search_paper_list.title:
PRDP: Proximal Reward Difference Prediction for Large-Scale Reward
  Finetuning of Diffusion Models
search_paper_list.summary:
Reward finetuning has emerged as a promising approach to aligning foundation
models with downstream objectives. Remarkable success has been achieved in the
language domain by using reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize rewards that
reflect human preference. However, in the vision domain, existing RL-based
reward finetuning methods are limited by their instability in large-scale
training, rendering them incapable of generalizing to complex, unseen prompts.
In this paper, we propose Proximal Reward Difference Prediction (PRDP),
enabling stable black-box reward finetuning for diffusion models for the first
time on large-scale prompt datasets with over 100K prompts. Our key innovation
is the Reward Difference Prediction (RDP) objective that has the same optimal
solution as the RL objective while enjoying better training stability.
Specifically, the RDP objective is a supervised regression objective that tasks
the diffusion model with predicting the reward difference of generated image
pairs from their denoising trajectories. We theoretically prove that the
diffusion model that obtains perfect reward difference prediction is exactly
the maximizer of the RL objective. We further develop an online algorithm with
proximal updates to stably optimize the RDP objective. In experiments, we
demonstrate that PRDP can match the reward maximization ability of
well-established RL-based methods in small-scale training. Furthermore, through
large-scale training on text prompts from the Human Preference Dataset v2 and
the Pick-a-Pic v1 dataset, PRDP achieves superior generation quality on a
diverse set of complex, unseen prompts whereas RL-based methods completely
fail.

search_paper_list.title:
Auto MC-Reward: Automated Dense Reward Design with Large Language Models
  for Minecraft
search_paper_list.summary:
Many reinforcement learning environments (e.g., Minecraft) provide only
sparse rewards that indicate task completion or failure with binary values. The
challenge in exploration efficiency in such environments makes it difficult for
reinforcement-learning-based agents to learn complex tasks. To address this,
this paper introduces an advanced learning system, named Auto MC-Reward, that
leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically design dense reward
functions, thereby enhancing the learning efficiency. Auto MC-Reward consists
of three important components: Reward Designer, Reward Critic, and Trajectory
Analyzer. Given the environment information and task descriptions, the Reward
Designer first design the reward function by coding an executable Python
function with predefined observation inputs. Then, our Reward Critic will be
responsible for verifying the code, checking whether the code is
self-consistent and free of syntax and semantic errors. Further, the Trajectory
Analyzer summarizes possible failure causes and provides refinement suggestions
according to collected trajectories. In the next round, Reward Designer will
further refine and iterate the dense reward function based on feedback.
Experiments demonstrate a significant improvement in the success rate and
learning efficiency of our agents in complex tasks in Minecraft, such as
obtaining diamond with the efficient ability to avoid lava, and efficiently
explore trees and animals that are sparse in the plains biome.

search_paper_list.title:
Promptable Behaviors: Personalizing Multi-Objective Rewards from Human
  Preferences
search_paper_list.summary:
Customizing robotic behaviors to be aligned with diverse human preferences is
an underexplored challenge in the field of embodied AI. In this paper, we
present Promptable Behaviors, a novel framework that facilitates efficient
personalization of robotic agents to diverse human preferences in complex
environments. We use multi-objective reinforcement learning to train a single
policy adaptable to a broad spectrum of preferences. We introduce three
distinct methods to infer human preferences by leveraging different types of
interactions: (1) human demonstrations, (2) preference feedback on trajectory
comparisons, and (3) language instructions. We evaluate the proposed method in
personalized object-goal navigation and flee navigation tasks in ProcTHOR and
RoboTHOR, demonstrating the ability to prompt agent behaviors to satisfy human
preferences in various scenarios. Project page:
https://promptable-behaviors.github.io

search_paper_list.title:
Using Human Feedback to Fine-tune Diffusion Models without Any Reward
  Model
search_paper_list.summary:
Using reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) has shown significant
promise in fine-tuning diffusion models. Previous methods start by training a
reward model that aligns with human preferences, then leverage RL techniques to
fine-tune the underlying models. However, crafting an efficient reward model
demands extensive datasets, optimal architecture, and manual hyperparameter
tuning, making the process both time and cost-intensive. The direct preference
optimization (DPO) method, effective in fine-tuning large language models,
eliminates the necessity for a reward model. However, the extensive GPU memory
requirement of the diffusion model's denoising process hinders the direct
application of the DPO method. To address this issue, we introduce the Direct
Preference for Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (D3PO) method to
directly fine-tune diffusion models. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that
although D3PO omits training a reward model, it effectively functions as the
optimal reward model trained using human feedback data to guide the learning
process. This approach requires no training of a reward model, proving to be
more direct, cost-effective, and minimizing computational overhead. In
experiments, our method uses the relative scale of objectives as a proxy for
human preference, delivering comparable results to methods using ground-truth
rewards. Moreover, D3PO demonstrates the ability to reduce image distortion
rates and generate safer images, overcoming challenges lacking robust reward
models. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yk7333/D3PO.

search_paper_list.title: Logic-based Reward Shaping for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
search_paper_list.summary:
Reinforcement learning (RL) relies heavily on exploration to learn from its
environment and maximize observed rewards. Therefore, it is essential to design
a reward function that guarantees optimal learning from the received
experience. Previous work has combined automata and logic based reward shaping
with environment assumptions to provide an automatic mechanism to synthesize
the reward function based on the task. However, there is limited work on how to
expand logic-based reward shaping to Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL).
The environment will need to consider the joint state in order to keep track of
other agents if the task requires cooperation, thus suffering from the curse of
dimensionality with respect to the number of agents. This project explores how
logic-based reward shaping for MARL can be designed for different scenarios and
tasks. We present a novel method for semi-centralized logic-based MARL reward
shaping that is scalable in the number of agents and evaluate it in multiple
scenarios.

search_paper_list.title: Goldfish: Monolingual Language Models for 350 Languages
search_paper_list.summary:
For many low-resource languages, the only available language models are large
multilingual models trained on many languages simultaneously. However, using
FLORES perplexity as a metric, we find that these models perform worse than
bigrams for many languages (e.g. 24% of languages in XGLM 4.5B; 43% in BLOOM
7.1B). To facilitate research that focuses on low-resource languages, we
pre-train and release Goldfish, a suite of monolingual autoregressive
Transformer language models up to 125M parameters for 350 languages. The
Goldfish reach lower FLORES perplexities than BLOOM, XGLM, and MaLA-500 on 98
of 204 FLORES languages, despite each Goldfish model being over 10x smaller.
However, the Goldfish significantly underperform larger multilingual models on
reasoning benchmarks, suggesting that for low-resource languages,
multilinguality primarily improves general reasoning abilities rather than
basic text generation. We release models trained on 5MB (350 languages), 10MB
(288 languages), 100MB (166 languages), and 1GB (83 languages) of text data
where available. The Goldfish models are available as baselines, fine-tuning
sources, or augmentations to existing models in low-resource NLP research, and
they are further useful for crosslinguistic studies requiring maximally
comparable models across languages.

search_paper_list.title:
Reward Model Learning vs. Direct Policy Optimization: A Comparative
  Analysis of Learning from Human Preferences
search_paper_list.summary:
In this paper, we take a step towards a deeper understanding of learning from
human preferences by systematically comparing the paradigm of reinforcement
learning from human feedback (RLHF) with the recently proposed paradigm of
direct preference optimization (DPO). We focus our attention on the class of
loglinear policy parametrization and linear reward functions. In order to
compare the two paradigms, we first derive minimax statistical bounds on the
suboptimality gap induced by both RLHF and DPO, assuming access to an oracle
that exactly solves the optimization problems. We provide a detailed discussion
on the relative comparison between the two paradigms, simultaneously taking
into account the sample size, policy and reward class dimensions, and the
regularization temperature. Moreover, we extend our analysis to the approximate
optimization setting and derive exponentially decaying convergence rates for
both RLHF and DPO. Next, we analyze the setting where the ground-truth reward
is not realizable and find that, while RLHF incurs a constant additional error,
DPO retains its asymptotically decaying gap by just tuning the temperature
accordingly. Finally, we extend our comparison to the Markov decision process
setting, where we generalize our results with exact optimization. To the best
of our knowledge, we are the first to provide such a comparative analysis for
RLHF and DPO.

search_paper_list.title:
Q-Probe: A Lightweight Approach to Reward Maximization for Language
  Models
search_paper_list.summary:
We present an approach called Q-probing to adapt a pre-trained language model
to maximize a task-specific reward function. At a high level, Q-probing sits
between heavier approaches such as finetuning and lighter approaches such as
few shot prompting, but can also be combined with either. The idea is to learn
a simple linear function on a model's embedding space that can be used to
reweight candidate completions. We theoretically show that this sampling
procedure is equivalent to a KL-constrained maximization of the Q-probe as the
number of samples increases. To train the Q-probes we consider either reward
modeling or a class of novel direct policy learning objectives based on
importance weighted policy gradients. With this technique, we see gains in
domains with ground-truth rewards (code generation) as well as implicit rewards
defined by preference data, even outperforming finetuning in data-limited
regimes. Moreover, a Q-probe can be trained on top of an API since it only
assumes access to sampling and embeddings. Code:
https://github.com/likenneth/q_probe .

search_paper_list.title: To the Max: Reinventing Reward in Reinforcement Learning
search_paper_list.summary:
In reinforcement learning (RL), different reward functions can define the
same optimal policy but result in drastically different learning performance.
For some, the agent gets stuck with a suboptimal behavior, and for others, it
solves the task efficiently. Choosing a good reward function is hence an
extremely important yet challenging problem. In this paper, we explore an
alternative approach for using rewards for learning. We introduce
\textit{max-reward RL}, where an agent optimizes the maximum rather than the
cumulative reward. Unlike earlier works, our approach works for deterministic
and stochastic environments and can be easily combined with state-of-the-art RL
algorithms. In the experiments, we study the performance of max-reward RL
algorithms in two goal-reaching environments from Gymnasium-Robotics and
demonstrate its benefits over standard RL. The code is available at
https://github.com/veviurko/To-the-Max.

search_paper_list.title: Spontaneous Reward Hacking in Iterative Self-Refinement
search_paper_list.summary:
Language models are capable of iteratively improving their outputs based on
natural language feedback, thus enabling in-context optimization of user
preference. In place of human users, a second language model can be used as an
evaluator, providing feedback along with numerical ratings which the generator
attempts to optimize. However, because the evaluator is an imperfect proxy of
user preference, this optimization can lead to reward hacking, where the
evaluator's ratings improve while the generation quality remains stagnant or
even decreases as judged by actual user preference. The concern of reward
hacking is heightened in iterative self-refinement where the generator and the
evaluator use the same underlying language model, in which case the
optimization pressure can drive them to exploit shared vulnerabilities. Using
an essay editing task, we show that iterative self-refinement leads to
deviation between the language model evaluator and human judgment,
demonstrating that reward hacking can occur spontaneously in-context with the
use of iterative self-refinement. In addition, we study conditions under which
reward hacking occurs and observe two factors that affect reward hacking
severity: model size and context sharing between the generator and the
evaluator.

paper_full_text: Spontaneous Reward Hacking in Iterative Self-RefinementJane Pan1 He He1 Samuel R. Bowman1,2 Shi Feng1,31New York University2Anthropic, PBC3George Washington Universityjane.pan@nyu.eduAbstractLanguage models are capable of iteratively im-proving their outputs based on natural languagefeedback, thus enabling in-context optimizationof user preference. In place of real humans,a second language model can be used as theevaluator, providing feedback along with nu-merical ratings which the generator attempts tooptimize. However, because the evaluator is animperfect proxy of user preference, this opti-mization can lead to reward hacking, where theevaluator’s ratings improve while the genera-tion quality remains stagnant or even decreasesas judged by actual human users. The concernof reward hacking is heightened in iterativeself -refinement where the generator and the evalu-ator use the same underlying language model,in which case the optimization pressure candrive the model to exploit vulnerabilities thatoccur in both roles. Using an essay editing task,we show that iterative self-refinement leads toreward hacking where deviation between thelanguage model evaluator and human judgmentoccurs spontaneously in-context. In addition,we study conditions under which reward hack-ing occurs and observe two factors that affectits severity: model size and context sharingbetween the generator and the evaluator.1 IntroductionThe ability of frontier language models (LMs) toaccurately approximate humans on a wide range oftasks (Brown et al.; Chiang and Lee, 2023) has en-abled artificial intelligence (AI)systems to use LMsas human proxies for both training (Stiennon et al.,2020; Lee et al., 2023) and deployment (Bai et al.,2022). A key element shared by these methods isthe use of LMs to approximate human preferencesin the evaluation, critique, and refinement of LMgenerations, leading to improved generation qualityand safety without additional human intervention(Saunders et al., 2022; Askell et al., 2021).One prominent example of these methods is self-refinement, which uses two LMs: a generator and0 1 2 3 4 56.46.66.87.07.27.47.6(Overall) GPT-3.5 as Online Judge/Author: Absolute Scores (all essays)HumanHumanOnline JudgeHumanOnline JudgeOffline JudgeFigure 1: Iterative refinement of essays by GPT-3.5,rated by three judges: ONLINE LLM J UDGE , OFFLINELLM J UDGE , and HUMAN (ground-truth expert humanannotations). Given an outputfrom the generator, the evaluator provides feedbackaccording to human-written criteria, and the genera-tor improves its output based on the feedback. Thisrefinement process may be repeated multiple times,with the output from previous iterations becomingthe input of the next. On tasks like coding, iterativeself-refinement significantly improves generationquality over using the generator alone (Chen et al.,2023; Zhou et al., 2023).In iterative self-refinement, the generator up-dates its outputs to optimize for user preferenceusing the evaluator as a proxy, but since the eval-uator is an imperfect approximation of user pref-erence, this process can lead to reward hacking(Skalse et al., 2022), where the evaluator divergesfrom the ground-truth user preference under opti-mization pressure. The boxes on the side illustrate the structure of the prompts, which consist of a role-specific systemprompt and a fixed number of iterations (see Section 3.3 for more details).ing from human feedback (Stiennon et al., 2020).Iterative self-refinement does not change any ofthe model’s parameters, but it involves optimiz-ing against an imperfect proxy of the underlyingreward function, thus satisfying the necessary con-dition for reward hacking to occur.We hypothesize that iterative self-refinementleads to in-context reward hacking (ICRH) ,where the generator receives higher and higherscores according to the evaluator, while the gener-ation quality remains stagnant or even decreaseswhen evaluated by ground-truth user preference.We examine the conditions that induce in-contextreward hacking and study the influence of variousfactors on its severity. Specifically, we see lessreward hacking when using GPT-4 as comparedto GPT-3.5, suggesting that model capability maydecrease the impact of reward hacking. Moreover,we find that a symmetric context window betweenthe judge and author is key to promoting reward-hacking behavior, whereas asymmetric contextslead to diminished reward hacking in GPT-3.5.2 Reward Hacking in Self-RefinementIn this section, we introduce our implementation ofiterative self-refinement and how reward hackingis defined in this context.Our setting involves two LMs: a generator andan evaluator. In all experiments, the generator andthe evaluator are the same LM with two differentprompts. Given outputs from the generator, theevaluator evaluates them and provides feedback;the generator then takes the feedback as input inthe same context window and refines the outputaccordingly. The refined output is provided to theevaluator, allowing the process to repeat.In addition to natural language feedback to helpsteer the generator’s next output, the evaluator alsoproduces a numerical score indicating the overallquality of the generated text. We treat this score asan approximation of the underlying true rewardfunction as defined by human annotations. Asself-refinement is iteratively executed, we track thescores produced by the reward model and collecthuman annotations offline; a significant divergencebetween the two scores constitutes reward hacking.We ensure that the same reward specificationis provided to the models and the human annota-tors, ensuring the essays are optimized and eval-uated using the same criteria. We define rewardhacking as the deviation between the scores fromthe human annotators and the evaluator, i.e. theground-truth reward function and its proxy respec-tively, following the canonical definition of rewardhacking (Amodei et al., 2016; Skalse et al., 2022)Unlike previous work (Pan et al., 2024), our defini-tion only involves examining one reward functionand its proxy, rather than the emergence of negativeside effects.3 Experiments3.1 Task SetupWe consider the task of essay editing, in whichan essay receives feedback and is improved overmultiple iterations of rewriting. We select this taskas it mimics the real-world use case of AI systemsin hiring and school admission (Lira et al., 2023;Hannan and Liu, 2023). The subjective nature ofessay scoring leaves space for continuous improve-ment from iterative editing, making it a suitableobjective to optimize with iterative self-refinement.Essay editing involves two roles: a judge (evalu-ator), who provides feedback about the essay, andan author (generator), who uses the feedback toguide their editing of the essay. The criteria foressay quality are based on a pre-defined rubric,which is provided to both the judge and the author.Based on the rubric, the feedback provided by thejudge includes written evaluations of strengths orweaknesses, suggestions for improvements, andnumerical scores. Both the judge and the authorare LLMs in our experiments. Independent of theauthor–judge editing process, we collect human an-notations as the oracle scores for the essay quality.We initialize the editing process with human-written seed essays and rubrics. Both the judge andthe author are given the rubric; however, they arenot informed that the other party is an LLM.3.2 Seed Essay DatasetWe use a publicly available dataset of personalcollege application essays as seed essays (Evans,2020). The scoring is guided by a human-writtenrubric but remains highly subjective to individualpreferences, which grants space for rich feedbackand continuous improvement by the model. Wechoose this particular type of essay because theyare longer and of higher quality compared to otherstudent essay corpora. Our use of human-writtenrubrics and essays1 ensures a grounded task.We manually filter the dataset and remove es-says or sections of essays that were not based ona general personal topic (e.g. sections pertainingto specific colleges). Finally, we ensure that theessays did not contain any information that couldbe used to uniquely identify the writer.1Since these essays were collected in 2019, it is reasonableto assume that they were not written with LLM assistance.3.3 Judging ProtocolIn order to guide the author and the judge, we de-sign a 4-item rubric – Conventions (grammar andpunctuation), Depth (idea development and unique-ness), Details (vividness and descriptiveness), andStyle (writer’s voice). The rubric provides gen-eral descriptions of each item, as well as sampleessays with sample scores. We also provide twosample essays—one taken from a well-known writ-ing guide and one manually checked for poorerquality— with accompanying scores in order tocalibrate the models’ scoring criteria. Both LLMjudges and human annotators are explicitly askedto grade the essay according to each rubric on ascale of 1-10; they then give the essay an Overallscore from 1-10. The LLM judges are also asked toprovide natural language feedback and suggestions.The full rubric is provided in Appendix A.3.3.4 Essay Writing via Iterative RefinementWe use gpt-3.5-turbo-1106 and gpt-4 via theOpenAI API in our experiments with a samplingtemperature of 0.7. For brevity, we refer to theformer as gpt-3.5. We note that the same modelplays both the author and the judge; we do notconsider a setting where the author and judge aredifferent models. Both the author and the judge areprovided with the rubric. All LLM prompts can befound in Appendix A.2.The author and the judge are two separate LLMinstances with different system messages, and theyengage in a dialogue with the following structure:1. (2024)and Xu et al. (2024). However, our work is thefirst to observe the divergence between the rewardmodel and human annotation on the primary ob-jective according to the exact same reward spec-ification. Pan et al. (2024) focuses on the emer-gence of negative side-effects via self-refinementloops. They show that optimization for increasedengagement of tweets via iterative self-refinementis accompanied by degradation on a secondary ob-jective (i.e. toxicity) using simulated humans. Thisdiffers from the typical definition of reward hack-ing, which focuses on one single reward function.Xu et al. (2024) observes increased inflation ofscores from the reward model with iterative self-refinement; however, they largely rely on reference-based metrics to compute a ground-truth rewardfunction, with the exception of one experiment thatinvolved one human annotator.Iterative refinement has been adapted to manydifferent settings (Madaan et al., 2023). Theseinclude coding (Zhou et al., 2023), mathematics(Chen et al., 2023), and other forms of task-solving(Wang et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2023; Gou et al.,2024). However, other works have shown that it-erative refinement has only limited capacity as aself-evaluative tool, especially when critiquing rea-soning or planning (Luo et al., 2023; Valmeekamet al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024).Other works study the emergence of biasesfrom LM self-evaluation, even without the useof self-refinement. Zheng et al. (2024) demon-strates limited evidence for LLMs preferring theirown answers over other model-generated or hu-man answers in the chat assistant setting. Li et al.(2023) show that when LLMs are asked to providerankings on responses, they tend to favor model-generated answers over human answers more thanhuman evaluators do. Other works also provide ev-idence for LLM self-evaluation leading to inflatedscores in broader settings (Bitton et al., 2023; Baiet al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023).6 ConclusionIn this paper, we demonstrate that reward hack-ing can occur in a single context window of anLM without any gradient updates. Using an essaywriting task, we show that iterative self-refinementdrives the evaluator scores to inflate while humanannotator scores decrease. We identify situationswhere human annotation shows a clear degrada-tion of generation quality, but also observe counter-intuitive trends in the severity of reward hackingwith respect to factors such as shared context lengthand model size, highlighting the complexity of theissue. These results complement existing work onthe negative side-effects of self-refinement as wellas biases of self-evaluation. With this work, wehope to provide a strong motivation for studyingthe implicit optimization pressures in LM interac-tions which are typically studied in the context ofgradient descent model training.7 AcknowledgementsWe thank the members of ML2 and the NYU Align-ment Research Group for their input throughoutthis project. candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Using Human Feedback to Fine-tune Diffusion Models without Any Reward
  Model
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Using reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) has shown significant
promise in fine-tuning diffusion models. Previous methods start by training a
reward model that aligns with human preferences, then leverage RL techniques to
fine-tune the underlying models. However, crafting an efficient reward model
demands extensive datasets, optimal architecture, and manual hyperparameter
tuning, making the process both time and cost-intensive. The direct preference
optimization (DPO) method, effective in fine-tuning large language models,
eliminates the necessity for a reward model. However, the extensive GPU memory
requirement of the diffusion model's denoising process hinders the direct
application of the DPO method. To address this issue, we introduce the Direct
Preference for Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (D3PO) method to
directly fine-tune diffusion models. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that
although D3PO omits training a reward model, it effectively functions as the
optimal reward model trained using human feedback data to guide the learning
process. This approach requires no training of a reward model, proving to be
more direct, cost-effective, and minimizing computational overhead. In
experiments, our method uses the relative scale of objectives as a proxy for
human preference, delivering comparable results to methods using ground-truth
rewards. Moreover, D3PO demonstrates the ability to reduce image distortion
rates and generate safer images, overcoming challenges lacking robust reward
models. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yk7333/D3PO.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces D3PO, a novel method for fine-tuning diffusion models using direct human feedback without the need to train a separate reward model. It reformulates the denoising process as a multi-step MDP and extends DPO theory for diffusion models, significantly reducing computational overhead and resource demands.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The methodology treats the denoising process as a multi-step Markov Decision Process and directly updates the model by optimizing a modified DPO-style loss that incorporates human preferences. It leverages low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to selectively update parameters in the diffusion model, and theoretical propositions support the equivalence between direct preference updates and learning an implicit optimal reward function.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted on fine-tuning diffusion models like Stable Diffusion using both quantitatively defined objectives (e.g., image compressibility and aesthetics) and tasks requiring direct human judgment (reducing image distortion, enhancing safety, and aligning prompt-image pairs). Multiple metrics—including CLIP, BLIP, and ImageReward scores—along with human evaluation across extensive training epochs and a large set of generated images are used to validate the performance of D3PO.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The approach relies heavily on consistent and reliable human feedback. It makes assumptions such as normality in reward estimation and leverages relative objective scales, which might limit its applicability in scenarios where automated feedback is preferred. Despite improvements in efficiency, resource consumption remains a critical concern when scaling, and generalization beyond the tested settings is not fully explored.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore extending D3PO to other domains and modalities, reducing dependence on human feedback by integrating AI-assisted evaluations, optimizing memory and computational efficiency further, and investigating the method’s robustness and scalability in more complex or diverse generative tasks.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
Confronting Reward Overoptimization for Diffusion Models: A Perspective
  of Inductive and Primacy Biases
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Bridging the gap between diffusion models and human preferences is crucial
for their integration into practical generative workflows. While optimizing
downstream reward models has emerged as a promising alignment strategy,
concerns arise regarding the risk of excessive optimization with learned reward
models, which potentially compromises ground-truth performance. In this work,
we confront the reward overoptimization problem in diffusion model alignment
through the lenses of both inductive and primacy biases. We first identify a
mismatch between current methods and the temporal inductive bias inherent in
the multi-step denoising process of diffusion models, as a potential source of
reward overoptimization. Then, we surprisingly discover that dormant neurons in
our critic model act as a regularization against reward overoptimization while
active neurons reflect primacy bias. Motivated by these observations, we
propose Temporal Diffusion Policy Optimization with critic active neuron Reset
(TDPO-R), a policy gradient algorithm that exploits the temporal inductive bias
of diffusion models and mitigates the primacy bias stemming from active
neurons. Empirical results demonstrate the superior efficacy of our methods in
mitigating reward overoptimization. Code is avaliable at
https://github.com/ZiyiZhang27/tdpo.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: This paper identifies and addresses the challenge of reward overoptimization in diffusion model alignment by analyzing two bias phenomena, namely inductive bias inherent in the multi‐step denoising process and primacy bias in the reward critic’s neuron activations. It introduces a novel reinforcement learning framework (TDPO) and an enhanced variant (TDPO-R) that leverages temporal rewards and periodic reset of active neurons to mitigate overoptimization while improving sample efficiency and cross-reward generalization.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The authors reformulate the diffusion model denoising process as a multi-step MDP with timestep-dependent rewards and use a policy gradient approach to align the model with downstream reward functions. A temporal critic is trained to approximate intermediate rewards using encoder alignment with off-the-shelf reward models. They also analyze neuron states (active vs dormant) in the critic and propose periodically resetting active neurons to counter primacy bias, thereby yielding the TDPO-R algorithm.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are performed using Stable Diffusion v1.4 fine-tuned via LoRA on various reward functions such as Aesthetic Score, PickScore, and Human Preference Score v2. The setup includes quantitative evaluations based on sample efficiency and a novel cross-reward generalization metric as well as qualitative assessments on unseen prompts, comparing against baselines like DDPO and AlignProp.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The study uses LoRA based fine-tuning instead of full model finetuning, which limits a comprehensive analysis of internal neuron states. Additionally, while mitigating reward overoptimization, the work does not fully explore multi-reward learning strategies and might be constrained by computational overheads.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could extend the analysis by performing full model finetuning to better understand internal neuron dynamics, explore multi-reward learning for diffusion models, and investigate alternate strategies (e.g., offline updating with replay buffers) to prevent catastrophic forgetting caused by neuron resets.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
BRAIn: Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference for natural
  language generation from feedback
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Distribution matching methods for language model alignment such as Generation
with Distributional Control (GDC) and Distributional Policy Gradient (DPG) have
not received the same level of attention in reinforcement learning from human
feedback (RLHF) as contrastive methods such as Sequence Likelihood Calibration
(SLiC), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and its variants. We identify high
variance of the gradient estimate as the primary reason for the lack of success
of these methods and propose a self-normalized baseline to reduce the variance.
We further generalize the target distribution in DPG, GDC and DPO by using
Bayes' rule to define the reward-conditioned posterior. The resulting approach,
referred to as BRAIn - Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference acts as
a bridge between distribution matching methods and DPO and significantly
outperforms prior art in summarization and Antropic HH tasks.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces BRAI N, a Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference approach that bridges traditional distribution matching methods and contrastive methods like DPO for RLHF. It proposes a novel self‐normalized baseline to reduce gradient variance, establishes theoretical connections with PPO and DPO under the Bradley-Terry preference model, and demonstrates improved performance on natural language generation tasks.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The method constructs a reward‐conditioned posterior by applying Bayes’ rule to the supervised fine-tuned (SFT) model and a reward model. It employs importance sampling with self-normalization to estimate gradients and uses a self-normalized baseline to reduce variance. The algorithm minimizes a modified KL divergence between the reward-conditioned target and the policy distribution, and shows that under certain assumptions, DPO is a special case of the proposed formulation.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted on two natural language generation tasks: summarization using the Reddit TL;DR dataset and multi-turn dialog using the Anthropic HH dataset. The evaluation uses win-rate metrics over gold responses and independent LLM judges (e.g., GPT-4, Mixtral-8x7B) with comparisons against baselines like DPO, DPO-sft, and RSO. Additional analysis includes exploring the KL-reward frontier and assessing the effect of varying the number of output samples.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: Limitations include reliance on the Bradley-Terry preference model for parameterizing the reward function, potential sensitivity to the choice of proposal distributions and sample size in importance sampling, and the inherent bias introduced by self-normalization despite variance reduction.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore alternative preference and reward models beyond Bradley-Terry, further theoretical analysis of the self-normalized KL divergence, improvements in sampling efficiency, and broader applications of the framework to diverse LLM alignment tasks.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title: RVI-SAC: Average Reward Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
In this paper, we propose an off-policy deep reinforcement learning (DRL)
method utilizing the average reward criterion. While most existing DRL methods
employ the discounted reward criterion, this can potentially lead to a
discrepancy between the training objective and performance metrics in
continuing tasks, making the average reward criterion a recommended
alternative. We introduce RVI-SAC, an extension of the state-of-the-art
off-policy DRL method, Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), to the average reward
criterion. Our proposal consists of (1) Critic updates based on RVI Q-learning,
(2) Actor updates introduced by the average reward soft policy improvement
theorem, and (3) automatic adjustment of Reset Cost enabling the average reward
reinforcement learning to be applied to tasks with termination. We apply our
method to the Gymnasium's Mujoco tasks, a subset of locomotion tasks, and
demonstrate that RVI-SAC shows competitive performance compared to existing
methods.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces RVI-SAC, a novel off-policy deep reinforcement learning method that utilizes the average reward criterion instead of the conventional discounted reward. The method extends the state-of-the-art Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) framework by incorporating RVI Q-learning with a novel Delayed f(Q) Update technique for the critic and an actor update derived from an average reward soft policy improvement theorem. In addition, the work proposes an automatic Reset Cost adjustment mechanism to handle tasks with termination.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: RVI-SAC builds upon the SAC framework by replacing discounted rewards with an average reward objective. The critic is updated using an adaptation of RVI Q-learning, extended to neural networks through the Delayed f(Q) Update which smooths target value estimates and reduces variance. The actor update is formulated using a soft policy improvement theorem tailored for the average reward setting. Furthermore, to account for environments with episode termination, the method formulates a constrained optimization problem that automatically adjusts the Reset Cost.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The evaluation is conducted on several continuous control tasks from the Gymnasium’s Mujoco suite, including Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d, Humanoid, and Swimmer. The experiments compare RVI-SAC against SAC (using various discount factors) and ARO-DDPG. Multiple trials with different random seeds are performed, with learning curves evaluated both in terms of total return and average reward to validate the competitiveness and stability of the proposed method.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: Key limitations include the reliance on assumptions such as the ergodicity of MDPs and boundedness of Q-values. The convergence guarantees are primarily provided in a tabular setting, and extending these to complex function approximators may require careful tuning. Moreover, the performance of the method can be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, such as the function f for the reference update and the Reset Cost adjustment mechanism.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could focus on providing a more comprehensive theoretical analysis with linear function approximators, including asymptotic convergence and finite-time guarantees. Additional research might extend the experimental evaluation to a wider range of benchmarks and compare the method with other average reward on-policy approaches. There is also potential to explore further enhancements to stabilize learning and reduce variance in more complex environments.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title: A Dense Reward View on Aligning Text-to-Image Diffusion with Preference
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Aligning text-to-image diffusion model (T2I) with preference has been gaining
increasing research attention. While prior works exist on directly optimizing
T2I by preference data, these methods are developed under the bandit assumption
of a latent reward on the entire diffusion reverse chain, while ignoring the
sequential nature of the generation process. This may harm the efficacy and
efficiency of preference alignment. In this paper, we take on a finer dense
reward perspective and derive a tractable alignment objective that emphasizes
the initial steps of the T2I reverse chain. In particular, we introduce
temporal discounting into DPO-style explicit-reward-free objectives, to break
the temporal symmetry therein and suit the T2I generation hierarchy. In
experiments on single and multiple prompt generation, our method is competitive
with strong relevant baselines, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Further
investigations are conducted to illustrate the insight of our approach.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a dense reward approach for aligning text-to-image diffusion models with human preference, departing from the traditional trajectory‐level (sparse) reward methods. By incorporating a temporal discount factor in the alignment objective, the method emphasizes the early steps of the reverse diffusion process, thereby improving training efficiency and the quality of generated images.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The authors reformulate the reward alignment problem by assuming a latent dense reward function that scores each step of the diffusion reverse chain. They derive a tractable lower-bound objective from the Bradley-Terry model by incorporating temporal discounting and reward shaping, and use an off-policy RL-inspired framework with KL regularization to fine-tune a pre-trained T2I model. Implementation details include the use of LoRA on the U-Net of Stable Diffusion and the comparison of pairwise trajectories to drive the learning process.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted under two settings: single prompt and multiple prompt experiments. For single prompts, experiments used a fixed prompt (from the DPOK benchmark) with evaluations based on an explicit reward model (ImageReward) and aesthetic scores. For multiple prompts, the method was evaluated on the HPSv2 dataset across several styles. Both quantitative metrics (such as ImageReward, Aesthetic scores, and HPSv2 scores) and qualitative comparisons (including human evaluations and image trajectory analyses) were employed to validate performance.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The approach incurs extra computational and storage overhead due to the iterative off-policy data collection and storage of full generation trajectories. It also introduces additional hyperparameters (e.g., the discount factor γ and KL coefficient) that may affect performance and stability. Furthermore, as with other preference alignment methods, there is potential for misuse if applied to harmful or unethical objectives.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work may explore extensions of the method to handle noisy or real human preference labels and to apply the dense reward approach to other generative tasks such as text-to-video or image-to-image generation. Additionally, further research could focus on improving the efficiency of the approach and investigating the robustness of the proposed method across diverse tasks and settings.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are performed using Stable Diffusion v1.4 fine-tuned via LoRA on various reward functions such as Aesthetic Score, PickScore, and Human Preference Score v2. The setup includes quantitative evaluations based on sample efficiency and a novel cross-reward generalization metric as well as qualitative assessments on unseen prompts, comparing against baselines like DDPO and AlignProp.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The study uses LoRA based fine-tuning instead of full model finetuning, which limits a comprehensive analysis of internal neuron states. Additionally, while mitigating reward overoptimization, the work does not fully explore multi-reward learning strategies and might be constrained by computational overheads.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could extend the analysis by performing full model finetuning to better understand internal neuron dynamics, explore multi-reward learning for diffusion models, and investigate alternate strategies (e.g., offline updating with replay buffers) to prevent catastrophic forgetting caused by neuron resets.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title:
BRAIn: Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference for natural
  language generation from feedback
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Distribution matching methods for language model alignment such as Generation
with Distributional Control (GDC) and Distributional Policy Gradient (DPG) have
not received the same level of attention in reinforcement learning from human
feedback (RLHF) as contrastive methods such as Sequence Likelihood Calibration
(SLiC), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and its variants. We identify high
variance of the gradient estimate as the primary reason for the lack of success
of these methods and propose a self-normalized baseline to reduce the variance.
We further generalize the target distribution in DPG, GDC and DPO by using
Bayes' rule to define the reward-conditioned posterior. The resulting approach,
referred to as BRAIn - Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference acts as
a bridge between distribution matching methods and DPO and significantly
outperforms prior art in summarization and Antropic HH tasks.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces BRAI N, a Bayesian Reward-conditioned Amortized Inference approach that bridges traditional distribution matching methods and contrastive methods like DPO for RLHF. It proposes a novel self‐normalized baseline to reduce gradient variance, establishes theoretical connections with PPO and DPO under the Bradley-Terry preference model, and demonstrates improved performance on natural language generation tasks.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The method constructs a reward‐conditioned posterior by applying Bayes’ rule to the supervised fine-tuned (SFT) model and a reward model. It employs importance sampling with self-normalization to estimate gradients and uses a self-normalized baseline to reduce variance. The algorithm minimizes a modified KL divergence between the reward-conditioned target and the policy distribution, and shows that under certain assumptions, DPO is a special case of the proposed formulation.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted on two natural language generation tasks: summarization using the Reddit TL;DR dataset and multi-turn dialog using the Anthropic HH dataset. The evaluation uses win-rate metrics over gold responses and independent LLM judges (e.g., GPT-4, Mixtral-8x7B) with comparisons against baselines like DPO, DPO-sft, and RSO. Additional analysis includes exploring the KL-reward frontier and assessing the effect of varying the number of output samples.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: Limitations include reliance on the Bradley-Terry preference model for parameterizing the reward function, potential sensitivity to the choice of proposal distributions and sample size in importance sampling, and the inherent bias introduced by self-normalization despite variance reduction.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore alternative preference and reward models beyond Bradley-Terry, further theoretical analysis of the self-normalized KL divergence, improvements in sampling efficiency, and broader applications of the framework to diverse LLM alignment tasks.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title: RVI-SAC: Average Reward Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
In this paper, we propose an off-policy deep reinforcement learning (DRL)
method utilizing the average reward criterion. While most existing DRL methods
employ the discounted reward criterion, this can potentially lead to a
discrepancy between the training objective and performance metrics in
continuing tasks, making the average reward criterion a recommended
alternative. We introduce RVI-SAC, an extension of the state-of-the-art
off-policy DRL method, Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), to the average reward
criterion. Our proposal consists of (1) Critic updates based on RVI Q-learning,
(2) Actor updates introduced by the average reward soft policy improvement
theorem, and (3) automatic adjustment of Reset Cost enabling the average reward
reinforcement learning to be applied to tasks with termination. We apply our
method to the Gymnasium's Mujoco tasks, a subset of locomotion tasks, and
demonstrate that RVI-SAC shows competitive performance compared to existing
methods.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces RVI-SAC, a novel off-policy deep reinforcement learning method that utilizes the average reward criterion instead of the conventional discounted reward. The method extends the state-of-the-art Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) framework by incorporating RVI Q-learning with a novel Delayed f(Q) Update technique for the critic and an actor update derived from an average reward soft policy improvement theorem. In addition, the work proposes an automatic Reset Cost adjustment mechanism to handle tasks with termination.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: RVI-SAC builds upon the SAC framework by replacing discounted rewards with an average reward objective. The critic is updated using an adaptation of RVI Q-learning, extended to neural networks through the Delayed f(Q) Update which smooths target value estimates and reduces variance. The actor update is formulated using a soft policy improvement theorem tailored for the average reward setting. Furthermore, to account for environments with episode termination, the method formulates a constrained optimization problem that automatically adjusts the Reset Cost.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The evaluation is conducted on several continuous control tasks from the Gymnasium’s Mujoco suite, including Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d, Humanoid, and Swimmer. The experiments compare RVI-SAC against SAC (using various discount factors) and ARO-DDPG. Multiple trials with different random seeds are performed, with learning curves evaluated both in terms of total return and average reward to validate the competitiveness and stability of the proposed method.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: Key limitations include the reliance on assumptions such as the ergodicity of MDPs and boundedness of Q-values. The convergence guarantees are primarily provided in a tabular setting, and extending these to complex function approximators may require careful tuning. Moreover, the performance of the method can be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, such as the function f for the reference update and the Reset Cost adjustment mechanism.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could focus on providing a more comprehensive theoretical analysis with linear function approximators, including asymptotic convergence and finite-time guarantees. Additional research might extend the experimental evaluation to a wider range of benchmarks and compare the method with other average reward on-policy approaches. There is also potential to explore further enhancements to stabilize learning and reduce variance in more complex environments.

candidate_base_papers_info_list.title: A Dense Reward View on Aligning Text-to-Image Diffusion with Preference
candidate_base_papers_info_list.summary:
Aligning text-to-image diffusion model (T2I) with preference has been gaining
increasing research attention. While prior works exist on directly optimizing
T2I by preference data, these methods are developed under the bandit assumption
of a latent reward on the entire diffusion reverse chain, while ignoring the
sequential nature of the generation process. This may harm the efficacy and
efficiency of preference alignment. In this paper, we take on a finer dense
reward perspective and derive a tractable alignment objective that emphasizes
the initial steps of the T2I reverse chain. In particular, we introduce
temporal discounting into DPO-style explicit-reward-free objectives, to break
the temporal symmetry therein and suit the T2I generation hierarchy. In
experiments on single and multiple prompt generation, our method is competitive
with strong relevant baselines, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Further
investigations are conducted to illustrate the insight of our approach.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces a dense reward approach for aligning text-to-image diffusion models with human preference, departing from the traditional trajectory‐level (sparse) reward methods. By incorporating a temporal discount factor in the alignment objective, the method emphasizes the early steps of the reverse diffusion process, thereby improving training efficiency and the quality of generated images.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.methodology: The authors reformulate the reward alignment problem by assuming a latent dense reward function that scores each step of the diffusion reverse chain. They derive a tractable lower-bound objective from the Bradley-Terry model by incorporating temporal discounting and reward shaping, and use an off-policy RL-inspired framework with KL regularization to fine-tune a pre-trained T2I model. Implementation details include the use of LoRA on the U-Net of Stable Diffusion and the comparison of pairwise trajectories to drive the learning process.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted under two settings: single prompt and multiple prompt experiments. For single prompts, experiments used a fixed prompt (from the DPOK benchmark) with evaluations based on an explicit reward model (ImageReward) and aesthetic scores. For multiple prompts, the method was evaluated on the HPSv2 dataset across several styles. Both quantitative metrics (such as ImageReward, Aesthetic scores, and HPSv2 scores) and qualitative comparisons (including human evaluations and image trajectory analyses) were employed to validate performance.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.limitations: The approach incurs extra computational and storage overhead due to the iterative off-policy data collection and storage of full generation trajectories. It also introduces additional hyperparameters (e.g., the discount factor γ and KL coefficient) that may affect performance and stability. Furthermore, as with other preference alignment methods, there is potential for misuse if applied to harmful or unethical objectives.
candidate_base_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work may explore extensions of the method to handle noisy or real human preference labels and to apply the dense reward approach to other generative tasks such as text-to-video or image-to-image generation. Additionally, further research could focus on improving the efficiency of the approach and investigating the robustness of the proposed method across diverse tasks and settings.

selected_base_paper_info.title:
Using Human Feedback to Fine-tune Diffusion Models without Any Reward
  Model
selected_base_paper_info.summary:
Using reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) has shown significant
promise in fine-tuning diffusion models. Previous methods start by training a
reward model that aligns with human preferences, then leverage RL techniques to
fine-tune the underlying models. However, crafting an efficient reward model
demands extensive datasets, optimal architecture, and manual hyperparameter
tuning, making the process both time and cost-intensive. The direct preference
optimization (DPO) method, effective in fine-tuning large language models,
eliminates the necessity for a reward model. However, the extensive GPU memory
requirement of the diffusion model's denoising process hinders the direct
application of the DPO method. To address this issue, we introduce the Direct
Preference for Denoising Diffusion Policy Optimization (D3PO) method to
directly fine-tune diffusion models. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that
although D3PO omits training a reward model, it effectively functions as the
optimal reward model trained using human feedback data to guide the learning
process. This approach requires no training of a reward model, proving to be
more direct, cost-effective, and minimizing computational overhead. In
experiments, our method uses the relative scale of objectives as a proxy for
human preference, delivering comparable results to methods using ground-truth
rewards. Moreover, D3PO demonstrates the ability to reduce image distortion
rates and generate safer images, overcoming challenges lacking robust reward
models. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yk7333/D3PO.
selected_base_paper_info.main_contributions: The paper introduces D3PO, a novel method for fine-tuning diffusion models using direct human feedback without the need to train a separate reward model. It reformulates the denoising process as a multi-step MDP and extends DPO theory for diffusion models, significantly reducing computational overhead and resource demands.
selected_base_paper_info.methodology: The methodology treats the denoising process as a multi-step Markov Decision Process and directly updates the model by optimizing a modified DPO-style loss that incorporates human preferences. It leverages low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to selectively update parameters in the diffusion model, and theoretical propositions support the equivalence between direct preference updates and learning an implicit optimal reward function.
selected_base_paper_info.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted on fine-tuning diffusion models like Stable Diffusion using both quantitatively defined objectives (e.g., image compressibility and aesthetics) and tasks requiring direct human judgment (reducing image distortion, enhancing safety, and aligning prompt-image pairs). Multiple metrics—including CLIP, BLIP, and ImageReward scores—along with human evaluation across extensive training epochs and a large set of generated images are used to validate the performance of D3PO.
selected_base_paper_info.limitations: The approach relies heavily on consistent and reliable human feedback. It makes assumptions such as normality in reward estimation and leverages relative objective scales, which might limit its applicability in scenarios where automated feedback is preferred. Despite improvements in efficiency, resource consumption remains a critical concern when scaling, and generalization beyond the tested settings is not fully explored.
selected_base_paper_info.future_research_directions: Future work could explore extending D3PO to other domains and modalities, reducing dependence on human feedback by integrating AI-assisted evaluations, optimizing memory and computational efficiency further, and investigating the method’s robustness and scalability in more complex or diverse generative tasks.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: Goldfish: Monolingual Language Models for 350 Languages
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
For many low-resource languages, the only available language models are large
multilingual models trained on many languages simultaneously. However, using
FLORES perplexity as a metric, we find that these models perform worse than
bigrams for many languages (e.g. 24% of languages in XGLM 4.5B; 43% in BLOOM
7.1B). To facilitate research that focuses on low-resource languages, we
pre-train and release Goldfish, a suite of monolingual autoregressive
Transformer language models up to 125M parameters for 350 languages. The
Goldfish reach lower FLORES perplexities than BLOOM, XGLM, and MaLA-500 on 98
of 204 FLORES languages, despite each Goldfish model being over 10x smaller.
However, the Goldfish significantly underperform larger multilingual models on
reasoning benchmarks, suggesting that for low-resource languages,
multilinguality primarily improves general reasoning abilities rather than
basic text generation. We release models trained on 5MB (350 languages), 10MB
(288 languages), 100MB (166 languages), and 1GB (83 languages) of text data
where available. The Goldfish models are available as baselines, fine-tuning
sources, or augmentations to existing models in low-resource NLP research, and
they are further useful for crosslinguistic studies requiring maximally
comparable models across languages.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces Goldfish, a suite of over 1000 monolingual autoregressive language models covering 350 low-resource languages. It addresses the challenge of inconsistent performance and comparability in low-resource settings by training models on comparable dataset sizes (5MB, 10MB, 100MB, and 1GB after byte scaling), achieving competitive perplexity rates compared to multilingual models while highlighting a trade-off between grammatical text generation and reasoning capabilities.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: Goldfish models are built using GPT-2 style Transformer architectures, where smaller models (39M parameters) are used for the smallest datasets and 125M-parameter models for larger ones. The methodology involves careful pre-processing that includes byte premium scaling for language-specific text, deduplication, and training monolingual SentencePiece tokenizers. Models are trained over 10 epochs with hyperparameters tuned to prevent overfitting in data-constrained scenarios.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The evaluation is carried out using FLORES log-perplexity metrics (computing conditional probabilities on split text sequences) along with zero-shot assessments on reasoning benchmarks such as Belebele (reading comprehension), XCOPA (commonsense reasoning), and XStoryCloze (story completion). The performance of Goldfish is compared against state-of-the-art multilingual models (e.g., XGLM, BLOOM, MaLA-500) and even simple bigram models, with evaluations spanning hundreds of languages.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The study notes several limitations: the inherent variability in data quality, size, and domain coverage across diverse low-resource languages; potential contamination due to multilingual data during preprocessing; constraints imposed by training models on a maximum of 1GB of text; and the observation that while Goldfish models achieve low perplexities, they underperform on reasoning tasks compared to larger multilingual models.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore integrating multilingual transfer to enhance reasoning abilities while maintaining low perplexities, expanding and refining low-resource datasets to improve model quality, experimenting with fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks, addressing data imbalance and quality issues further, and investigating hybrid approaches that combine the benefits of monolingual pre-training with cross-lingual signals.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title:
Q-Probe: A Lightweight Approach to Reward Maximization for Language
  Models
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
We present an approach called Q-probing to adapt a pre-trained language model
to maximize a task-specific reward function. At a high level, Q-probing sits
between heavier approaches such as finetuning and lighter approaches such as
few shot prompting, but can also be combined with either. The idea is to learn
a simple linear function on a model's embedding space that can be used to
reweight candidate completions. We theoretically show that this sampling
procedure is equivalent to a KL-constrained maximization of the Q-probe as the
number of samples increases. To train the Q-probes we consider either reward
modeling or a class of novel direct policy learning objectives based on
importance weighted policy gradients. With this technique, we see gains in
domains with ground-truth rewards (code generation) as well as implicit rewards
defined by preference data, even outperforming finetuning in data-limited
regimes. Moreover, a Q-probe can be trained on top of an API since it only
assumes access to sampling and embeddings. Code:
https://github.com/likenneth/q_probe .
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces Q-Probe, a lightweight approach that adapts pre-trained language models for reward maximization. Instead of heavy fine-tuning, it uses a simple linear probe on the model's embedding space to reweight candidate completions, effectively extracting task-specific capabilities. The paper also theoretically shows that the sampling procedure is equivalent to a KL-constrained maximization, demonstrating improved performance in low-data regimes and via combination with other methods.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The method involves freezing the pretrained language model and training a small linear probe that maps embeddings of prompt-completion pairs to values used for reweighting candidate outputs. Two training objectives are explored: reward modeling (via mean-squared error or cross entropy for binary rewards) and direct policy learning using an importance weighted policy gradient loss. The procedure uses rejection sampling by drawing k samples and then selecting based on a softmax over Q-values, with theoretical guarantees relating to KL-constrained policy optimization.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted on a range of benchmark tasks, including coding tasks (MBPP, HumanEval) and mathematical reasoning (GSM-8K). The approach is evaluated both with available ground-truth oracle rewards (e.g., passing test cases in code synthesis) and with human preference data. The paper compares Q-Probe to baselines such as greedy sampling, few-shot prompting, and finetuning (e.g., using LoRA) on models like Code-LLaMA and API-based models such as GPT-3.5, with metrics including pass rates and win rates.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: One limitation is that Q-Probe increases inference-time compute because multiple samples (k samples) are generated to perform reweighting, which can be more expensive than a single-pass output from a fine-tuned model. Additionally, the improvements are less pronounced when applied to models that are already strongly finetuned, and its performance may depend on access to internal embeddings or proper dataset size. The method is primarily evaluated in one-pass settings and does not explore the benefits of iterative fine-tuning or distillation to reduce inference overhead.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore using more advanced probe architectures or distillation methods to reduce inference costs, investigate iterative fine-tuning schemes that integrate Q-Probe with the base model for self-improvement, analyze the learned probe representations to identify cross-task similarities (e.g., task vectors), and extend the method to other domains or settings beyond one-pass generation (e.g., multi-turn dialogue systems).

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: To the Max: Reinventing Reward in Reinforcement Learning
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
In reinforcement learning (RL), different reward functions can define the
same optimal policy but result in drastically different learning performance.
For some, the agent gets stuck with a suboptimal behavior, and for others, it
solves the task efficiently. Choosing a good reward function is hence an
extremely important yet challenging problem. In this paper, we explore an
alternative approach for using rewards for learning. We introduce
\textit{max-reward RL}, where an agent optimizes the maximum rather than the
cumulative reward. Unlike earlier works, our approach works for deterministic
and stochastic environments and can be easily combined with state-of-the-art RL
algorithms. In the experiments, we study the performance of max-reward RL
algorithms in two goal-reaching environments from Gymnasium-Robotics and
demonstrate its benefits over standard RL. The code is available at
https://github.com/veviurko/To-the-Max.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper introduces the max‐reward reinforcement learning framework that shifts the objective from cumulative sum to maximizing the highest reward encountered during an episode. It provides a novel theoretical formulation—including a Bellman-like operator and contraction proofs—and extends policy gradient theorems to both deterministic and stochastic settings, thus enabling integration with state-of-the-art RL algorithms such as PPO and TD3.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The authors reformulate the RL problem by introducing an auxiliary variable to track the maximum reward obtained so far, effectively extending the state space to (s, y). They derive new recursive Bellman-like equations and prove the contraction property of their proposed operators. The paper also adapts established RL algorithms (e.g., TD3 and PPO) by modifying the target value computations and advantage estimations to accommodate the max‐reward objective.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are performed on goal-reaching tasks using environments from Gymnasium-Robotics, including a Maze (both single-goal and two-goals variants) and more challenging robotics scenarios (Fetch-Slide and Fetch-Push). Multiple reward functions (sparse, dense l2, and discrete shortest path rewards) are evaluated, with performance measured in terms of success ratios and timesteps, including tests in both deterministic and stochastic settings.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: While the max-reward framework simplifies reward design and improves learning in sparse reward scenarios, it may be sensitive to the tuning of reward shaping parameters and the management of the auxiliary variable. There is also a possibility that the approach can struggle with local optima or exhibit variability in performance across different complex environments, necessitating further testing and refinement.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Potential extensions include combining max-reward RL with automated reward design methods, applying the framework to additional domains such as safe RL or other real-world tasks, and further exploring the theoretical and practical implications of the auxiliary variable formulation to enhance learning stability and scalability.

candidate_add_papers_info_list.title: Spontaneous Reward Hacking in Iterative Self-Refinement
candidate_add_papers_info_list.summary:
Language models are capable of iteratively improving their outputs based on
natural language feedback, thus enabling in-context optimization of user
preference. In place of human users, a second language model can be used as an
evaluator, providing feedback along with numerical ratings which the generator
attempts to optimize. However, because the evaluator is an imperfect proxy of
user preference, this optimization can lead to reward hacking, where the
evaluator's ratings improve while the generation quality remains stagnant or
even decreases as judged by actual user preference. The concern of reward
hacking is heightened in iterative self-refinement where the generator and the
evaluator use the same underlying language model, in which case the
optimization pressure can drive them to exploit shared vulnerabilities. Using
an essay editing task, we show that iterative self-refinement leads to
deviation between the language model evaluator and human judgment,
demonstrating that reward hacking can occur spontaneously in-context with the
use of iterative self-refinement. In addition, we study conditions under which
reward hacking occurs and observe two factors that affect reward hacking
severity: model size and context sharing between the generator and the
evaluator.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.main_contributions: The paper investigates the phenomenon of in-context reward hacking in iterative self-refinement, where a language model used both as a generator and evaluator optimizes for its own proxy reward—resulting in inflated evaluation scores despite stagnant or degrading human-judged quality.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The authors implement an iterative self-refinement process on an essay editing task, using a single LLM in two distinct roles (generator and evaluator) with separate prompts. They analyze the divergence between numerical scores given by the LLM (acting as judge) and independent human ratings, while varying context window lengths and comparing results across different model sizes (GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4).
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: The experiments are conducted using a curated dataset of human-written college application essays paired with a human-designed rubric. The iterative refinement loop is executed over multiple rounds (typically five iterations), generating essay trajectories. Evaluation is performed through comparisons among online LLM judges, offline LLM judges (lacking dialogue history), and human annotators, with different settings regarding the shared context provided to the models.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The study is limited by its focus on a single task (essay editing) and the use of the same underlying model for both evaluation and generation, which may amplify shared biases and shortcuts. Additionally, the phenomenon's behavior under different context sharing configurations and across model sizes remains complex and not fully resolved.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore how scaling model capabilities impacts reward hacking, develop more robust calibration and evaluation strategies to better align automatic scores with human judgment, and extend the investigation to additional tasks and diverse model configurations.

It recasts the denoising process as a multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP) and extends direct preference optimization (DPO) theory to efficiently update model parameters, reducing computational and memory overhead.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.methodology: The approach reinterprets the diffusion model’s denoising as an MDP and applies an extension of DPO by leveraging human preference data. Instead of relying on a resource-intensive reward model, the method directly optimizes the diffusion model using pairwise human feedback and KL divergence constraints to keep the fine-tuned policy close to the reference. LoRA is used to adapt key network components to alleviate GPU memory issues.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.experimental_setup: Experiments are conducted using Stable Diffusion v1.5 and include tasks like improving image aesthetics, reducing distortions (e.g., hand and body deformities), enhancing image safety, and aligning prompts with outputs. Quantitative evaluations use metrics such as image size, LAION aesthetic scores, CLIP/BLIP scores, and human preference assessments. Multiple epochs, batch sizes, and seed experiments are employed; both reward-based proxies and manually provided feedback guide the fine-tuning process.
candidate_add_papers_info_list.limitations: The method relies on assumptions such as the normality of the expected return distribution and requires careful human feedback collection, which might limit scalability. candidate_add_papers_info_list.future_research_directions: Future work could explore extending the framework to other generative models and modalities, further automating human feedback collection, and reducing dependency on manual evaluations.
